The session begins.

Morning reaches Beregost before it reaches your room. First come the hammers, one forge and then another, until the whole town rings like a slow bell. Then the creak of a laden cart on the Trade Way, a mule complaining, and the smell of bacon and new bread rising through the floorboards from the kitchen below.

The shutters let in a thin blade of daylight. It falls across the chest at the foot of the bed, across your pack and your gear, and across the cat. The cat is sitting on the windowsill and not looking at the street. It is looking at a single copper coin that stands upright on the sill, balanced on its edge, perfectly still. You don't remember leaving it there.

The purse is where you left it, heavy with the last hand you'll ever win. Nothing is asked of you today. No contract, no caravan, no debt to settle before noon. Baldur's Gate is still days up the road.

On the stairs outside, footsteps climb, unhurried, and stop at your door. A woman's voice comes through the wood: "Master Worgen? You're awake, I hope. There's porridge going and a man downstairs asking whether the gentleman with the cat is still lodging here."

The cat's tail flicks once. The coin does not fall.

Hedda's keys clink against the doorframe as she shifts her weight. "Respectable can wait till after porridge. Half the men down there aren't either."

Before she answers your question, the cat does. Its voice arrives inside your head the way it always does, unhurried and a little bored, as if it had been asked something obvious.

*Not mine. I don't push coins about.* Its ears stay pinned toward the sill. *It was standing when the light came in. I've been waiting for it to fall. It hasn't.*

A pause, and then, more quietly: *I didn't hear anyone put it there. I would have.*

The copper stays where it is in the thin strip of sun, standing on its rim, its face turned toward the shutters and away from you. Dust drifts slowly past it in the light. Nothing in the room moves except the cat's tail.

"Tallow," Hedda says through the door. "Corwin Tallow, he said. Young, thin, road dust up to the knees. Says he walked in from the north before the gates were properly open." Her tone makes it plain she doesn't think much of anyone who walks before breakfast. "Wouldn't take porridge. Wouldn't take ale. He's sitting by the hearth with his hat on his knee, asking after a man with a cat. Not your name, mind. The cat." The keys clink again. "Shall I tell him you're coming down, or tell him you've gone?"

You place it on the second look. It's a wave breaking both ways, Umberlee's sign, the Queen of the Depths. You saw it on the docks at Zazesspur when you were young and in Zaranda's colours: deckhands cutting that curl into coppers before they sailed, then throwing the coins over the side as the ship cleared harbour. It was a small toll paid to the sea so she'd let them come back. A coin cut like that belongs in the water. The sailors you knew wouldn't pick one up off a quay, never mind keep it. They said it meant you'd taken something that was already promised to her.

It isn't the Lady's face, or the Lady's coin. And Beregost is a long day's ride from salt water.

The copper keeps standing on its rim in the strip of sun, perfectly level, ship to the window and wave to you. When you breathe out, the dust shifts around it. The coin doesn't move.

*That isn't hers,* the cat says. It hasn't looked away from the coin once. *Your Lady's. I'd know her smell. This smells like nothing at all.*

Its tail stays still for a moment.

*Nothing at all smells like nothing.*

Downstairs a bench scrapes, and you hear Hedda's voice, too low to make out, then a younger man answering her, quick and polite.

It takes a few minutes to dress: shirt, studded leather, the old regimental cloak, the rod and the Lady's coin where your hand can find them. When you open the door the copper is still standing on the sill in its strip of sun. You leave it there and close the door on it.

The cat goes down the stairs ahead of you, one step at a time, tail up.

The common room of the Anvil and Ember is half full and mostly quiet at this hour. Two carters are bent over their bacon. A caravan guard is asleep sitting up, with his boots on the bench. Hedda comes out of the kitchen as you reach the bottom step. She sets two bowls of porridge and a heel of new bread on the table nearest the hearth, gives you a look that says *both of them, mind*, and goes back to her ovens.

The young man by the fire stands up too quickly and nearly drops his hat.

He can't be much past twenty. He's thin the way people get when they skip meals, not when they're born that way. His hair is straw-coloured and his face is chapped from the wind. There are pale crusts of old wax on his cuffs, and the toe of one boot is tied shut with twine. He looks at the cat before he looks at you, and for a little longer.

*Tallow and road dust,* the cat says, settling on the warm hearthstones. *And a long night without sleep. He smells like a person.* It says that as if it ought to be obvious, and after this morning maybe it is.

"Master Worgen." He works the hat brim round in his fingers. "Corwin Tallow. From the Gate, the Lower City. My father makes candles off the Wide." He swallows. "I'm sorry to come at you before you've eaten. I didn't have your name till Mistress Marrow said it. All I had was the cat."

He glances at the cat again, as if it might vanish.

"I went to the Lady's Hall about my brother. There's an old priestess there, Mother Ysolde. She threw the coins for me, and when she'd looked at them she said to walk south on the Way till I met a man coming north with a cat. She said he'd be the Lady's own, and I'd know him." He gives a short laugh with no humour in it. "I've asked at every inn between the Friendly Arm and here. Three days of it. Folk thought I was simple. You're the first man who's had a cat."

He doesn't sit down. His knuckles have gone white on the hat.

"Is it true? Are you hers?"

Corwin's eyes go to the coin before you've finished drawing it. It's only in sight for a moment, the Lady's face worn soft with handling, and then it's back where your hand keeps it. He lets out a breath he seems to have been holding since the Friendly Arm.

He sits down on the very edge of the bench, the way a man sits who expects to be asked to leave. The bowl is in front of him now. He doesn't pick up the spoon. He puts both hands around the bowl, as if all he wants from it is the warmth, and looks at the bread you've broken without taking any of it.

"Pell," he says. "Pell Tallow. He's two years older than me. He was." He stops, and the hat brim goes round once in his fingers on his knee. "Sorry. I still say *is*. He was a porter on the docks. He never wanted the candle trade. Said he couldn't stand the smell of it."

He looks at the hearth instead of at you.

"Twelve days ago the Fist pulled him out of the harbour by the Grey Harbour steps. They had me come to the Seatower to say it was him." He says it flat, the way you say something you've already told a dozen people who didn't listen. "There was a copper in his mouth, pushed in behind his teeth. It had that mark cut on it, the sailors' one for the sea. The sergeant laughed and said the Bitch Queen had been paid, then. They wrote him down as drink. Fell in drunk, drowned, done."

His jaw tightens.

"Pell drank like any porter does. He could also swim like an eel. He used to dive off the end of the quays for coppers the sailors threw when we were boys."

Then he says the next part more slowly, as if he's worried you'll laugh at it the way the sergeant did.

"Three nights before, he came to supper at our father's and told it as a joke. He'd come home and found a copper standing up on his table. On its edge. Just standing there. He said he blew on it and it didn't fall, so he left it for luck and went to bed laughing." A short laugh, with nothing behind it. "He said it was the best luck he'd ever had, a coin that wouldn't lie down. After, when I went to his room for his things, there wasn't a coin on the table. Nothing at all."

On the hearthstones the cat has gone completely still. Its ears aren't on Corwin any more. They're turned back toward the stairs, toward the room above.

*His brother had one,* it says. Then, after a moment, more quietly: *Upstairs we have one.*

Corwin doesn't see any of that. He's looking at his hands around the bowl.

"Mother Ysolde didn't laugh," he says. "She threw the coins three times, and the third time she went white, and she sent me down the Way to find you. She didn't say why. She just said I'd know you." He looks up, and his eyes stay on you. "I don't want money from you. I want somebody to find out who put a coin in my brother's mouth."

Corwin doesn't move when you say *copper*. When you say *same mark*, the bowl tilts in his hands and a little porridge slops over the rim onto the table. He doesn't notice.

"Upstairs," he says. "In this house."

He looks at the ceiling, and then at you, the way a man looks at someone who has just told him he's standing on rotten ice. The hat has stopped turning on his knee.

"I'm sorry. I shouldn't say it like this." He swallows. "Pell laughed at his. Three nights, and then they pulled him out at the Grey Harbour steps. You should get out of here, away from it. Or throw it in the fire, or... I don't know what you're meant to do." He stops, because he can hear that he doesn't know, and his voice drops. "You said you'd help. I didn't walk three days to get you killed as well."

On the hearthstones the cat has turned its head from the stairs to Corwin.

*He's frightened for you,* it says. *That's new. Most people are frightened of you.*

Corwin pulls in a breath, puts the bowl down carefully and wipes his hand on his knee. Then he makes himself answer what you asked, slowly, the way he must have gone through it alone every night since.

"No trouble that I know of. Not the kind you mean. He owed a few silver to a dice man on the Wide. Everybody does. The Guild takes its cut at the steps the same as anywhere, and Pell paid it like everyone else. Nobody hated him. He was too loud to hate. You just told him to shut up."

His brow tightens.

"But there was work. That same week. A ship came in early, a Calishite cog called the *Brightwater*, out of Calimport. The porters were all talking about her. She was nine days ahead of when anyone expected her, and the men on the quay said she'd had the wind dead behind her the whole way up the coast, like something was pushing her. Pell hauled her cargo for two days. Good money. Double." He lets out a short breath. "Except the purser paid it all in copper, out of a sack. A whole sack of coppers. Pell grumbled about it at supper, said his purse weighed more than the crates."

He looks at his hands.

"Her crew never came ashore. Pell thought that was odd. Sailors nine days early with a pocket full of pay, and not one of them in the taverns. He said they just stood along the rail and watched the porters work." He shakes his head. "He made a joke of that too. He made a joke of everything."

Then, more quietly:

"The coin on his table. He found it the night after the *Brightwater* paid off. I never put those two things together till now." He looks up at you. "Is that something? Or am I just looking for a reason?"

Corwin turns the question over before he answers. You can see him doing it honestly, checking what he actually knows and leaving out what he'd like to be true.

"I don't know about the other porters," he says at last. "I should. I didn't ask." He looks down at the bowl. "After the Seatower I just went home and sat with Father. I didn't think to go round the steps and count heads."

He stops, and then goes on.

"There's one thing. The sergeant who laughed. He didn't say it like a joke he'd just made up. He said it the way you say something you've said before, the way you say 'mind the step' to someone. *The Bitch Queen's been paid, then.* Like he'd pulled others out with coppers in their mouths and stopped thinking it was strange." His jaw works. "At the time I just wanted to hit him. I didn't think about what he meant."

The hat goes round once on his knee and then stops.

"Pell worked her with Haskin Dree. Big man, ginger, they'd carried together on the Grey Harbour steps for years. Haskin was at the burial. He stood at the back and didn't say a word, and Haskin talks more than Pell did. I thought it was grief." Corwin's voice drops. "He'd know who else hauled for the *Brightwater*. If anyone does."

As for the ship, he shakes his head slowly.

"She was still in when I left. Not at the quay, though. They'd warped her off and she was riding at anchor out past the Grey Harbour moorings, waiting on a return cargo, the harbour men said. She was still sitting there the morning I went up to the Lady's Hall. That's..." He counts it on his fingers under the table. "Four days ago. Maybe five. I don't know if she's sailed since."

He seems to notice the bowl for the first time. He picks up the spoon, eats one mouthful like he's doing it because he was told to, and puts the spoon down again.

On the hearthstones the cat has its chin on its paws now, but its eyes are open.

*A ship that waits for cargo with a crew that won't come ashore,* it says. *Somebody is paying for every day she sits there.*

Corwin wipes his mouth and looks at you. The fear from before hasn't gone. He has only put it to one side so he could answer you.

"Master Worgen. What will you do about the one upstairs?"

"I'll be here," he says. He looks at the second bowl as if it's been set in front of him to test him, and then, after a moment, he picks up the bread.

The copper hasn't moved at all. It still stands on its rim, ship toward the window and the cut wave toward the door, toward where you stand.

You keep an arm's length back and go down on your heels to look at it the way you'd look at a ward on a tomb door. You check the coin, the wood under it and the air around it, and you go through everything you know that could make a thing stand where it shouldn't.

You start with the ordinary explanations, the way you were taught to. There's no shimmer at the coin's edges when you shift your head, so it isn't an illusion pretending to be a coin. Nothing tugs at the air near it either, none of the faint pressure an invisible hand or a bound servant leaves around itself, and no cantrip would still be holding after a whole night. You look for runes cut into the sill, chalk, wax or a drawn circle, and find none.

That's where your knowledge runs out. Whatever is holding the copper up, you can't put a name to it. It doesn't match any working you studied or any you've seen another caster use. The best you can say is what it isn't, and that list doesn't tell you much.

Your eyes catch one thing, though. Now that you're level with the sill and the sun is at a lower angle, you can see a thin pale line on the dark wood around the coin's foot. It's a ring no wider than a thumbnail, crusted white, the kind of mark seawater leaves on a deck plank once it dries. It wasn't there this morning, or you couldn't see it in that light. You can't say which.

The cat jumps onto the far end of the sill, comes along it with its belly low and puts its nose close to the white line, closer than you'd let it. It holds still there for a long breath.

*Salt ought to smell of salt,* it says.

It backs away along the sill, one paw at a time.

*That doesn't.*

Out on the Trade Way a cart rolls past below the window. The hammers have found their rhythm across the town. In the strip of sun, the copper stands on its rim and doesn't fall.

You turn the key in the lock and test the door once with your shoulder. It holds. The cat watches you do it and says nothing.

Hedda is at the foot of the stairs with a basket of eggs on her hip. When you lower your voice she lowers hers to match. She's run an inn on the Trade Way long enough to know which conversations carry.

The keys at her belt go still while she hears you out. Her eyes go up to the ceiling, toward your room, and come back down to you.

"Nobody goes in," she says. "Not the girl, not me, nobody." She shifts the basket to her other hip. "But I'll say this once, Master Worgen. If it's the sort of dangerous that burns, or smells, or comes through the floor, you tell me before it does. I've a roof to think of, and eleven other beds under it." Her mouth twitches. "Not that most of them would be any loss."

She goes back to her kitchen without waiting for an answer.

Corwin is still at the table by the hearth when you cross the common room. One bowl is empty now and the bread is half gone. He looks up and starts to rise. Then he sees you're dressed for the street and sits again, both hands flat on the table, as if he's holding himself down.

---

Beregost is louder outside than it sounded from upstairs. The forges along the main street have their doors open to the morning. Every few yards the clang of a hammer comes out over the cobbles, with heat behind it and a smell of hot iron and wet charcoal. A smith's boy runs past carrying a bundle of horseshoes on a cord. Two ox-carts heading south have locked wheels at the corner by the cooper's, and the drivers are explaining each other's mothers to the whole street. The cat walks the edge of the boardwalk with its tail up and steps around a puddle like it has a grudge against it.

The Song of the Morning sits at the eastern edge of town, where the houses thin into kitchen gardens. It's built of pale stone with tall windows facing the sunrise, and the dome is roofed in copper gone green. Dawn prayers are long over. The great doors are pinned open and a scatter of townsfolk are coming down the steps: a carter's wife with a sleeping baby, two journeymen smiths still in their aprons, an old man leaning on a boy's arm. Inside, the morning light comes through rose-coloured glass and lies across the floor in long warm panels.

*Incense,* the cat says on the top step. *Roses. Lamp oil. Old men's feet.* Its whiskers come forward. *Everything in here smells of something.*

A woman is working her way down the nave, gathering the morning's offerings from the foot of the altar. There are posies of field flowers, a loaf, a few candle-ends, a child's carved horse. She's in her forties, broad in the shoulder, wearing the rose-and-gold vestment of Lathander's clergy with the sleeves pushed up past the elbow, and an old white scar runs along one forearm. She sets the carved horse carefully back where it was, picks up the posies, and sees you standing in the doorway with a cat at your heel.

Hedda is behind the counter with a slate. She's already chalking the figures before you reach her.

"Room for the night, five silver. Two breakfasts, one each, never mind who ate what. That's two more." She turns the slate round for you to see. "Seven silver. I'm not charging for the morning's excitement. I'd not know what to put."

You set a gold piece on the board. She takes it, digs three silver out of the strongbox under the counter and puts them in your palm. When you thank her, her keys clink once.

"You told me straight, Master Worgen. That's worth something in this house." She glances across the common room at a man asleep with his mouth open in the corner. "More than I can say for some."

Sister Aubren is on her feet by the hearth with the satchel strap on her shoulder and the stone jug against her hip. She lets you say your goodbye and nods.

"Go well, Master Worgen. You too," she adds, to the cat, which looks back at her steadily and for once doesn't look bored. She turns to Corwin's empty place at the table, then to you. "Look after that lad. He walked three days on hope and very little bread." She shifts the jug. "And I'll be watching the carters."

She goes out into the noise of the street. Hedda watches her down the steps before she goes back to her slate.

The yard is busier than it was. Both teams are in the traces now, four oxen to each wagon, shifting their weight and blowing. Corwin is at the head of the second team with his blanket roll slung across his back. He's holding a lead rope in the careful way of someone who has been told exactly how to hold it and wants to get it right. Ottar is beside him in a dented half-helm with a short spear across his shoulders. He's pointing at something on the near ox's yoke and talking.

"...and if she swings her head like that, you let her. Don't pull against her. She's bigger than you." He sees you and nods once. "Worgen. Your lad's not useless. That's more than I expected."

Corwin goes red to the ears and doesn't let go of the rope.

Pryor is walking the length of the lead wagon, tugging each rope where it crosses the bales and marking his tablet. He sees you come out with your pack, looks at the cat, and says nothing at all. On the box of the second wagon Mistress Pryor has moved her basket aside to leave a space on the bench beside her. She hasn't said who it's for.

The cat looks the wagons over, chooses the rear of the second one, and jumps lightly onto the tailboard. It walks up to the bales and stops just short of the sacking. Then it sits down on the bare plank with its tail tucked neatly round its feet, touching no wool at all.

*He said he'd charge for the bale,* it says. *He said nothing about the board.*

The sun climbs. Somewhere along the main street a hammer stops, then another, as the smiths break for their bread. At the Song of the Morning, at the far end of town, the bell begins to ring noon.

Pryor puts the tablet inside his coat. "That's it," he says to nobody in particular, and climbs heavily onto the box of the lead wagon. Ottar walks to the yard gate and swings it wide. Corwin hands back the lead rope as he's been told, scrambles onto the tailboard beside the cat and sits with his knees drawn up, looking north up the Way.

Pryor shakes the reins. The oxen lean into the yokes, the axles groan, and the wool wagons roll out of the Anvil and Ember's yard onto the Trade Way, heading for the Gate.

The oxen walk slowly and evenly, the axles complain every few turns, and the Way runs north between hayfields and hedges with the dust lying low over it. You fall in beside Ottar at the lead team's shoulder. Your feet remember the old rhythm before you do: a long step, an easy swing, eyes on the next rise in the road. It's the pace a column keeps when it knows it will still be walking at dusk.

Ottar notices. He doesn't say anything for a good fifty feet, but his eyes go to your stride, then to the cloak, then back to the road.

"Tonight's Hollin's Ford," he says when you ask. "There's no inn. It's a drovers' ground on the near bank of a stream, with a stone ring for a fire and a well the farmer up the slope lets you use if you give him a copper. With oxen we'll get there about an hour short of dark, if Pryor doesn't stop to count his bales again." He shifts the spear across his shoulders. "Tomorrow night's the Friendly Arm, and that's the wall and the beer. Day after, the Gate by evening, if the axles hold. The left rear one on the second wagon's been talking since Nashkel."

On the second question he takes longer. He spits into the ditch first.

"This stretch? Not much. Not the way it is south of Beregost." He jerks his chin back the way you came. "Down toward Nashkel they're losing whole trains, wagons, guards and all, and nobody can say who's taking them. That's why Pryor's paying me double and I'm sleeping in my boots." He walks a few paces. "Up here it's mostly the usual. Some lads with clubs who think a wool wagon's an easy mark until they see a spear. Wolves now and then, nearer the Arm. The Fist used to ride this road twice a week. Now I see them maybe twice a month, and they're always in a hurry going somewhere else."

His half-helm turns a little toward you. He isn't looking at the road now.

"I've been doing this nine years, Worgen. I can tell what lads with clubs look like coming at you. I don't know what your sort of trouble looks like." He keeps his voice down, below the creak of the wagons. "Hedda had the whole house checking its windowsills this morning, and then the Lathander woman came down your stairs looking like she'd carried a sack of iron up them. Pryor says you told him straight. Fair enough. He didn't tell me anything." He shifts his grip on the spear. "So I'm asking. If it comes at us on this road, what am I meant to be looking for?"

Behind you, on the tailboard of the second wagon, the cat has opened one eye.

*He's been wanting to ask that since the yard,* it says. *He waited until the wife couldn't hear.*

Ottar hears you out without looking at you. He watches the road, the hedges and the next rise, the way a man listens when he's putting a list together in his head. When you say *stood on edge by itself*, his stride checks for half a step and then picks up again.

"Standing coin. Salt. Somebody looking at you or the lad too long." He says it back under his breath, like a man repeating a price so he won't forget it. "Don't touch the coin. Right."

He walks on for a while. A hay cart passes going south, and the driver lifts a hand. Ottar lifts his back and waits until it's well behind before he speaks again.

"Knives I know. Somebody follows a train for a day, he gets careless at the water stops. He stands too long at the same well as you, or he's on the same road you are and slower than he needs to be." He glances back once at the tailboard, where Corwin is sitting with his knees up and the cat beside him, both looking north. "The other kind I don't know. I'll tell you if I see anything that doesn't fit, and you can tell me what it is."

On the ford he answers quickly. This part is his trade.

"Hollin's stream is low this time of year. You'd wet your boots, no more than that." He thinks about it for a moment. "A drunk can drown in less, mind. Pryor likes the wagons drawn up on the flat by the water so the oxen don't have far to go. We'll water them first, then pull up the slope under the farmer's hedge. It's a longer walk for a piss, and the farmer's dogs are closer." He nods once, satisfied with that. "Dogs bark at anybody coming up from the water in the night. That's worth something to me."

He doesn't say whether he'll tell Pryor why. You suspect he'll call it the dogs.

Back on the tailboard the cat has turned one ear toward the two of you.

*He believed you,* it says. *He doesn't know what to believe, so he picked the parts he can watch for.* The ear turns forward again. *That's what you did too.*

The wagons roll on. The Way climbs a long, gentle rise between fields of stubble, and Beregost's hammers fade behind you until all you can hear is the axles, the oxen and the dust. Up ahead the road runs north into the afternoon.

The afternoon goes by at an ox's pace. The Way climbs out of the stubble fields into rougher grazing land, dips through a stand of alders where the dust lies thick and pale, and climbs again. You keep your place at the lead team's shoulder and watch the road and the hedgerows. You see a magpie on a gatepost, a shepherd's boy a long way off with his flock spread over a hillside, and a milestone so weathered you can't read the number. No coins. No one standing too long anywhere.

About midafternoon three Flaming Fist riders come down the Way from the north at a hard trot, cloaks dusty to the hip. They pull over to pass the wagons. The one in front looks along the train, at Ottar, at your cloak, at the bales, and doesn't slow down. Ottar watches them go until they're specks.

"Twice a month," he says, to nobody in particular.

A little later Mistress Pryor turns on the box of the second wagon and looks back at the tailboard. Corwin is still sitting on it with his knees up, and his head has started to drop and jerk up again, drop and jerk up. She watches this happen twice. Then she pats the empty bench beside her.

"Young man." It's the first thing you've heard her say. Her voice is dry and quiet. "You'll go off that board asleep and under my wheel, and then I'll have that to think about as well. Come up here."

Corwin jerks awake, goes red, apologises to her, apologises again to the cat for some reason, and climbs over the bales onto the box. He sits as far toward the edge as he can without falling off. Within half a mile he's asleep with his chin on his chest. Mistress Pryor moves her basket onto her other knee and doesn't look at him again.

On the tailboard the cat has the whole plank to itself now. It spreads out across it.

*So that's who the seat was for,* it says. *She waited until he was tired enough to say yes.*

---

You reach Hollin's Ford with the sun low and red behind the hills to the west, about the hour short of dark that Ottar promised. The Way runs down a long slope to a shallow stream, brown and quick over gravel and no deeper than your boot. The near bank opens into a trampled flat of grass with a blackened ring of fire-stones in the middle and plenty of old ox-dung. Up the slope a hawthorn hedge, thick and old, runs along the top of a farm field. Behind it there's a low stone farmhouse with smoke coming from its chimney. Two dogs come down along the far side of the hedge as the wagons roll in. They're rough-coated and grey-muzzled, and they bark once each, the way dogs do when they mean *we see you*.

The water smells of water. The cat goes down to the edge, sniffs it, and comes back up without saying anything about it.

Ottar does just what he said he would. The oxen go down to the stream first, two at a time, and drink with their noses deep in the current. Pryor climbs down off the box and starts toward the flat by the fire-ring. Ottar says something to him quietly, and it ends with the word *dogs*. Pryor looks up the slope at the hedge, then at the farmhouse, and grunts. The wagons go up.

It takes a while to get them up there. The left rear axle on the second wagon complains the whole way. By the time both wagons are drawn up under the hawthorn and chocked, and the oxen are hobbled on the grass between, the sun has gone. The sky is turning the colour of a bruise in the west. An old man has come out of the farmhouse with a lantern to stand at the gap in the hedge and look you all over. Pryor walks up and puts a copper in his hand for the well. They talk about the price of wool without either of them seeming to enjoy it.

Ottar builds a fire up under the hedge rather than down in the old ring by the water. While it's catching he squats beside you and feeds it twigs.

"Watches," he says. "Three of them. I'll take first, while the Pryors are still moving about, and last, because the oxen get restless before dawn and I know them." He snaps a stick and puts it on. "You've got the middle. It's the worst one. I know that." He glances at you. "But if anything comes up from that water, I'd sooner it was you awake than me. I wouldn't know what I was looking at."

Up on the box of the second wagon Corwin is waking up slowly. He's blinking at the fire, and doesn't seem to know where he is yet.

messages.text:
“Awake, yes. Respectable, not quite. Did the gentleman give a name?”

I keep my eyes on the copper and ask the cat silently, *Was that your doing, or have we received instructions before breakfast?*

“Tell him I'll be down shortly. And I'll take the breakfast he wouldn't.”

I crouch beside the sill to look at the copper's face and reverse without touching it. “All right, my Lady,” I murmur. “You have my attention.”
[Roll the die]
[Onward]

*Then let's leave it where it is. I've lost enough money without borrowing trouble from the sea.*

I finish dressing, take my gear, and head downstairs with the cat to meet Corwin Tallow.

“Master Tallow? I'm James Worgen. I hear you've been asking after my companion.”

“I am.” I draw the worn silver coin briefly into view, then sit and push the second bowl toward him.

“Sit down, Corwin. Eat what you can. You've found us; you can stop walking for a moment.”

I break the bread between us. “Tell me about your brother. What's his name, and what's happened to him?”

“I'm sorry, Corwin. Your brother deserved better than a laugh and a line in a ledger. I'll help you find out.”

I set my spoon down.

“There's something you should know. This morning I found a copper standing on edge in my room. Same mark. It's still upstairs. I haven't touched it.”

I give him a moment before asking, “Between finding his coin and that last supper—did Pell mention unusual work, trouble on the docks, or anyone he'd offended?”

“It's something worth following. Not proof, but a ship arriving impossibly early, a crew that won't come ashore, and that payment—I want to know more.”

I lean forward. “Did any of the other porters who worked the *Brightwater* turn up drowned or go missing? And do you know whether she's still in the harbour?”

“Not throw it in Hedda's fire and hope that improves matters. We don't know what it does—or whether moving it is what someone wants.”

I stand. “I'll take another look, then seek help at the Song of the Morning. A priest may recognise something I don't. Stay here and eat, Corwin. You haven't brought this on me.”

*Come on,* I tell the cat. *Let's see whether it's changed.*

I return upstairs, keeping clear of the copper while I examine it and the surrounding sill for anything my knowledge of magic might explain.
[Roll the die]
[Onward]

I lock the room behind us and tell Hedda quietly, “There's something in my room that may be dangerous. Please don't let anyone in to clean until I've spoken with the temple.”

Then I head to the Song of the Morning with the cat, seeking a priest who can advise me about a possibly cursed coin.

“James Worgen. I serve Tymora, though this morning I'm in need of advice.”

I keep my voice low. “A copper appeared on my windowsill overnight, standing on edge. It won't fall, and it bears Umberlee's mark. There's a white crust around its base, like dried seawater. I've left it untouched and locked the room.”

“A visitor from Baldur's Gate tells me his brother found just such a coin. Three nights later he was pulled from the harbour with a marked copper behind his teeth. I can't identify the magic, and I don't want to endanger an inn full of people by experimenting.”

“Would you come and examine it, Sister?”

“No. I warned the innkeeper to keep everyone out of my room, but I didn't ask about the others. I should have.”

I glance toward the street. “I'll go ahead and ask Hedda to check with her guests—without touching any coin they find. We'll meet you at the Anvil and Ember.”

I head back with the cat to do exactly that.

“I don't know, Hedda. It hasn't burned, smelled, or moved, but I can't promise it won't. That's why I've brought Sister Aubren. Thank you for checking the rooms.”

I introduce Aubren to Hedda and Corwin, then lead her upstairs and unlock my door.

“The copper is on the sill. Nothing's touched it since I found it.” I stand aside to let her examine it.

“Try to break it. Whoever offered me to the sea already knows who I am. I'd rather they learn I'm objecting.”

I move back from the sill and call the cat to my side.

“And I'll still go after whoever did the asking. Pell didn't have this warning, or someone willing to help him.”

“Then it goes to the sea when I reach the Gate. Not into Hedda's well or a stream someone drinks from.”

I take an empty pouch from my pack. “Is it safe to carry now? If so, I'll keep it separate until I can return it.”

I look at her marked palm. “Thank you, Sister. You put yourself between me and something ugly. I won't forget that.”

Once the coin is safely dealt with, I head downstairs to tell Hedda and Corwin what happened and discuss the road north.

“Of course you can come, Corwin. You've walked far enough alone.”

To Aubren, I add, “You'll have that letter as soon as I have a name.”

Then I go out to the yard to find Pryor. “Master Pryor? James Worgen. I'm looking for passage to the Gate for two men and a cat. What would you charge?”

“The copper is coming with me, wrapped and separate from my money. Someone laid a hostile prayer on it, aimed at me. Sister Aubren broke that prayer this morning; she's inside if you'd rather hear it from her.”

I meet his eyes. “She believes it's an ordinary toll coin now, to be returned to the sea. But whoever sent it may know it was broken, and I can't promise they won't try again. You deserve to know that before taking us aboard.”

“If you'll still have us, four gold is fair, and I'll stand with Ottar if trouble comes.”
[Roll the die]
[Onward]

“You'll hear it from me first.” I count four gold into his palm.

Then I return to Corwin. “We've got passage. Noon bell, ready by the wagons—Pryor means it. Have you anything to collect before we go?”

“Go on. I'll be right behind you.”

I settle any outstanding charge for my room and breakfast with Hedda, thank her for her help, and bid Sister Aubren farewell. Then I join Corwin at the wagons with my pack and the cat, ready for the road north.

I walk alongside Ottar, settling into the old marching rhythm and keeping an eye on the road ahead.

“Where are we stopping tonight? And have you had any trouble on this stretch lately?”

“I wish I could give you a face to watch for. Someone sent me a copper bearing Umberlee's mark. It stood on edge by itself, with salt gathering beneath it. Corwin's brother found one like it before he drowned in the Gate.”

I keep my voice low. “Sister Aubren broke the prayer on mine. Whoever made it felt her do it. Whether that means hired knives, more magic, or nothing on this road, I don't know.”

“If you see a coin standing where it shouldn't, unexplained seawater, or anyone taking an unusual interest in me or the lad, tell me. Don't touch the coin. I'll tell you and Pryor if I notice anything.”

I glance back toward the second wagon. “At the ford, let's keep the sleeping places well back from the water.”

“Good thinking. I'll take my share of the watch tonight.”

With that settled, I keep pace beside the wagons, watching the road and hedges as we make for Hollin's Ford.

The opening worked well for me. A coin standing on edge was a small, memorable mystery, and Corwin’s account made it personal without needing a fight. I chose to help him because I cared about what happened to Pell. James’s connection to Tymora gave him a reason to listen without taking that choice away.

The NPCs were the strongest part. Hedda protecting her inn, Aubren admitting the limits of her help, Pryor weighing an honestly disclosed risk, and his wife quietly giving Corwin a safer seat all felt believable. My decisions mattered: telling the truth affected passage, consulting a priest changed the coin, and warning Ottar changed the campsite. That made quiet play satisfying.

What broke:
- **The dice were using the wrong modifiers.** Every displayed check used +2, including Persuasion, which should be +7. The correct skill appeared in the label but not the calculation. That needs fixing before a consequential roll fails.
- **Records sometimes contradicted the scene.** Locations were added or changed as though I had travelled somewhere merely because it was mentioned. Attunement was also tracked despite the campaign’s explicit exception.
- **Pacing dragged.** Several brief exchanges consumed ten or fifteen minutes, and simple actions often received long recaps. The prose was good, but repeating the coin’s stillness, Corwin’s hat-turning, and everyone’s meaningful pauses diluted their effect.

What was missing was clearer mechanical grounding for the magical investigation. Aubren’s intervention was dramatically effective, but I couldn’t tell what spell she used or what rules governed the danger. Mystery is welcome; unexplained magic shouldn’t become the default replacement for the agreed 5e rules. Likewise, a failed Arcana check confidently ruled out several explanations without making clear how James knew those things.

The cat had personality and useful observations, though it commented so often that it sometimes interpreted NPCs for me before I could form my own impression. A little more silence would help.

Overall, I wanted to continue. Keep the grounded NPCs, consequences, and room for noncombat decisions. Fix the roll integration and state tracking, and tighten routine narration so more choices fit into a session.

Yes—when Aubren said the intact coin was a thread leading back to whoever made it. I wanted to ask, **“Can we actually follow that thread? What would keeping it intact let us do?”**

Instead, I chose to break it. The danger was concrete—Pell died after three nights—but the investigative opportunity wasn’t. I couldn’t tell whether preserving the coin meant a usable lead or simply waiting for something bad to happen. With an inn full of bystanders, breaking it felt like the only responsible choice.

I liked that dilemma. One more concrete detail about what investigating the intact link might involve would have made it a harder, more informed decision—not necessarily a safer one.

Up close it's an ordinary copper, the kind every purse on the Trade Way carries a dozen of. It's thin, a little bent and dark with handling. On the face toward the shutters there's a ship under sail, worn soft at the edges, the kind of stamp they press by the thousand on the coast. You lean round to see the other side, still without touching it, and find the reverse rubbed almost smooth. Someone has scratched a mark into the smooth patch with a knife point or a nail: one line that rises, curls over on itself and drops away to both sides.

You've seen that sign somewhere. You try to place it.

You place it on the second look. It's a wave breaking both ways, Umberlee's sign, the Queen of the Depths. You saw it on the docks at Zazesspur when you were young and in Zaranda's colours: deckhands cutting that curl into coppers before they sailed, then throwing the coins over the side as the ship cleared harbour. It was a small toll paid to the sea so she'd let them come back. A coin cut like that belongs in the water. The sailors you knew wouldn't pick one up off a quay, never mind keep it. They said it meant you'd taken something that was already promised to her.

It isn't the Lady's face, or the Lady's coin. And Beregost is a long day's ride from salt water.

The copper keeps standing on its rim in the strip of sun, perfectly level, ship to the window and wave to you. When you breathe out, the dust shifts around it. The coin doesn't move.

*That isn't hers,* the cat says. It hasn't looked away from the coin once. *Your Lady's. I'd know her smell. This smells like nothing at all.*

Its tail stays still for a moment.

*Nothing at all smells like nothing.*

He glances at the cat again, as if it might vanish.

He doesn't sit down. His knuckles have gone white on the hat.

"Is it true? Are you hers?"

"I'll be here," he says. He looks at the second bowl as if it's been set in front of him to test him, and then, after a moment, he picks up the bread.

The cat is already on the stairs ahead of you.

The room is as you left it. The narrow bed, the chest, the shutters with daylight laid across the boards. The strip of sun has moved a hand's width along the sill since you went down. The copper hasn't moved at all. It still stands on its rim, ship toward the window and the cut wave toward the door, toward where you stand.

You keep an arm's length back and go down on your heels to look at it the way you'd look at a ward on a tomb door. You check the coin, the wood under it and the air around it, and you go through everything you know that could make a thing stand where it shouldn't.

You start with the ordinary explanations, the way you were taught to. There's no shimmer at the coin's edges when you shift your head, so it isn't an illusion pretending to be a coin. Nothing tugs at the air near it either, none of the faint pressure an invisible hand or a bound servant leaves around itself, and no cantrip would still be holding after a whole night. You look for runes cut into the sill, chalk, wax or a drawn circle, and find none.

That's where your knowledge runs out. Whatever is holding the copper up, you can't put a name to it. It doesn't match any working you studied or any you've seen another caster use. The best you can say is what it isn't, and that list doesn't tell you much.

Your eyes catch one thing, though. Now that you're level with the sill and the sun is at a lower angle, you can see a thin pale line on the dark wood around the coin's foot. It's a ring no wider than a thumbnail, crusted white, the kind of mark seawater leaves on a deck plank once it dries. It wasn't there this morning, or you couldn't see it in that light. You can't say which.

The cat jumps onto the far end of the sill, comes along it with its belly low and puts its nose close to the white line, closer than you'd let it. It holds still there for a long breath.

*Salt ought to smell of salt,* it says.

It backs away along the sill, one paw at a time.

*That doesn't.*

Out on the Trade Way a cart rolls past below the window. The hammers have found their rhythm across the town. In the strip of sun, the copper stands on its rim and doesn't fall.

Hedda is at the foot of the stairs with a basket of eggs on her hip. When you lower your voice she lowers hers to match. She's run an inn on the Trade Way long enough to know which conversations carry.

The keys at her belt go still while she hears you out. Her eyes go up to the ceiling, toward your room, and come back down to you.

"Nobody goes in," she says. "Not the girl, not me, nobody." She shifts the basket to her other hip. "But I'll say this once, Master Worgen. If it's the sort of dangerous that burns, or smells, or comes through the floor, you tell me before it does. I've a roof to think of, and eleven other beds under it." Her mouth twitches. "Not that most of them would be any loss."

She goes back to her kitchen without waiting for an answer.

---

Beregost is louder outside than it sounded from upstairs. The forges along the main street have their doors open to the morning. Every few yards the clang of a hammer comes out over the cobbles, with heat behind it and a smell of hot iron and wet charcoal. A smith's boy runs past carrying a bundle of horseshoes on a cord. Two ox-carts heading south have locked wheels at the corner by the cooper's, and the drivers are explaining each other's mothers to the whole street. The cat walks the edge of the boardwalk with its tail up and steps around a puddle like it has a grudge against it.

The Song of the Morning sits at the eastern edge of town, where the houses thin into kitchen gardens. It's built of pale stone with tall windows facing the sunrise, and the dome is roofed in copper gone green. Dawn prayers are long over. The great doors are pinned open and a scatter of townsfolk are coming down the steps: a carter's wife with a sleeping baby, two journeymen smiths still in their aprons, an old man leaning on a boy's arm. Inside, the morning light comes through rose-coloured glass and lies across the floor in long warm panels.

*Incense,* the cat says on the top step. *Roses. Lamp oil. Old men's feet.* Its whiskers come forward. *Everything in here smells of something.*

A woman is working her way down the nave, gathering the morning's offerings from the foot of the altar. There are posies of field flowers, a loaf, a few candle-ends, a child's carved horse. She's in her forties, broad in the shoulder, wearing the rose-and-gold vestment of Lathander's clergy with the sleeves pushed up past the elbow, and an old white scar runs along one forearm. She sets the carved horse carefully back where it was, picks up the posies, and sees you standing in the doorway with a cat at your heel.

She takes in the soldier's cloak, the rod at your belt, the cat. She doesn't hurry, and she doesn't look away either.

"You've missed dawn prayers by about two hours, friend," she says, and comes up the nave toward you with the flowers in the crook of her arm. "If you've come for those, there's always tomorrow. The Morninglord isn't fussy about late starts." She stops a few paces off. "But you don't look like you've come to pray. I'm Sister Aubren. What's the trouble?"

“James Worgen. I serve Tymora, though this morning I'm in need of advice.”

I keep my voice low. “A copper appeared on my windowsill overnight, standing on edge. It won't fall, and it bears Umberlee's mark. There's a white crust around its base, like dried seawater. I've left it untouched and locked the room.”

“A visitor from Baldur's Gate tells me his brother found just such a coin. Three nights later he was pulled from the harbour with a marked copper behind his teeth. I can't identify the magic, and I don't want to endanger an inn full of people by experimenting.”

turns.reply:
Sister Aubren listens without interrupting. When you say *standing on edge*, her eyes go to your face and stay there. When you say *Umberlee*, the posies in the crook of her arm stop rustling. By the time you reach the harbour and the copper behind the teeth, the easy morning look has gone from her face. What's left is attentive and a good deal older.

She doesn't answer straight away. She turns, walks back down the nave to the altar and lays the field flowers at its foot, stems together, beside the loaf and the carved horse. Then she comes back up to you, wiping her palms on her vestment.

"I'll come," she says. "I won't promise you anything when I get there. You'll want to know why."

She keeps her voice as low as yours. A man is sweeping the far aisle.

"I've seen the Bitch Queen's coppers. Anyone who's worked a ferry crossing or a river caravan has. Sailors cut them and throw them over the side, and her priestesses come round the quays with a bowl and take what's owed. It's an ugly bargain, but it's an honest one. You pay the sea so it lets you go home." She shakes her head slowly. "I've never heard of one standing up by itself, a long day from salt water, in a room nobody went into. And I've never heard of the sea sending its bill to a man before it's come to collect."

She glances down at the cat, then back at you.

"If someone has laid a working on that coin, the Morninglord has given me ways to take it apart, and I'll try. If it's a mark that came from her and not from a man, I may not be able to touch it, and I'll tell you so rather than pretend. Better you know that now than stand in your room hoping."

She's already pushing her sleeves higher. Her eyes go to the door, toward the street and the forges, and the Anvil and Ember somewhere beyond them.

"Give me a few minutes. I'll fetch water from the font and my things." Halfway through turning away, she stops. "Master Worgen. You said it's an inn full of people. Do you know whether anyone else in that house woke up to find a coin this morning?"

*She's right to ask,* it says. *You should have.* After a few steps: *I should have too.*

The common room of the Anvil and Ember has emptied a little. The carters have gone and their plates are stacked. The caravan guard is awake now and lacing his boots. Corwin is still at the hearth table, sitting straight with both hands round an empty cup. He half rises when he sees you and reads your face before you reach him.

You find Hedda in the kitchen doorway with flour to the elbows. You tell her quietly what you need. She listens the way she did on the stairs, with her keys still.

"Coppers," she says. "Standing up on their edges. And nobody's to touch one if they find it." She wipes her hands on her apron, slowly, front and back. "If I ask that of a wool merchant and his wife before they've had their eggs, Master Worgen, they'll think I've gone soft in the head. I'll ask it anyway."

She goes up. The cat goes too, along the upstairs passage. It walks slowly with its nose low and stops at every door. You can feel it working through the threshold cracks: old boots, tallow, someone's lavender water, a chamber pot nobody has emptied.

It takes the best part of a quarter of an hour. You hear knocking, voices through the floor, and a man's laugh that stops short. At one point Hedda says sharply, "Then *look*, Master Pryor, it's a windowsill, not a riddle." A door closes harder than it needs to.

The cat comes back down first and sits by your boot.

*Seven doors,* it says. *Everything behind them smells of something. Nothing smells of nothing.* Its ears go up toward the ceiling, toward the room at the end that's yours. *Except where we left it. Same as before. No more and no less.*

Hedda comes down behind it, counting on her floury fingers.

"Pryor and his wife, nothing but a bad temper. The two pilgrims out of Amn, nothing. They said a prayer at me, which I didn't ask for. "The third room she hadn't got to. I went in myself just now. Sill's bare. Dust on it, no salt."

She looks at you, and then up at the ceiling again.

"So it's you, Master Worgen. Only you, under my roof." The keys clink once as she shifts her weight. "Now. You told me to be warned before it burns or stinks or comes through the floor. Is it that kind, or isn't it?"

At the hearth Corwin has put the cup down. He heard every word.

Out in the street a woman's voice says something to the smith's boy, and he answers with a laugh. Sister Aubren comes through the open door with a stoppered stone jug against her hip and a canvas satchel over one shoulder. She stops just inside, looks over the room, and finds you.

"Objecting," she says. "Well. That's one way to put it." She glances at him over her shoulder. "Pell didn't have anyone. You've got a stubborn woman with a jug. Stand where you are, please, and keep the cat back. I don't know which way this'll kick."

She unhooks the sunrise disc from her neck and wraps the chain twice around her scarred hand so the disc sits flat against her palm. Still on one knee, she holds it level with the coin about a foot from the white ring, the way you'd hold a lamp up to read a worn inscription. Then she starts to pray. It isn't a chant. She speaks low and plainly, like someone at a door explaining why they need to come in. The light through the shutters doesn't change, but the rose-gold disc starts to look warmer than the sun on it can explain.

Nothing happens at first. Then the coin begins to ring.

It's barely audible, a thin high note like a wet finger round the rim of a glass, and it's coming out of the copper. The white ring around its foot darkens. It goes grey, then wet, and the wet spreads across the sill in a slow stain. It runs toward the window and away from Aubren, and the smell finally reaches you: brine, weed, the cold green smell under a pier at low tide. The cat's fur stands up along its spine.

Aubren's breath goes short. Sweat comes out along her hairline. Her hand with the disc in it shakes once, and she brings the other hand up under her wrist to hold it level, the way a man braces a crossbow. She keeps talking, lower now, and you catch one word of it: "*No.*"

The note stops.

The copper tips. It doesn't drop like a stone. It leans slowly, the way a sleeper's head falls forward, then goes over and lands flat on the sill with the small dull click any coin makes. It rocks once and lies still with the ship side up.

The wet stain is already drying at the edges. What's left is a scatter of ordinary grey-white grit, the kind a bucket of harbour water leaves behind.

Aubren lets her breath go and sits back on her heels. She unwinds the chain from her hand slowly. The links have pressed red marks into her palm.

"It's done. The asking's broken." She wipes her forehead with the back of her wrist. "It was close, I'll tell you that for nothing. Whoever made it knew their business. That wasn't some deckhand with a knife and a grudge."

She looks at the copper lying flat, and then at you.

"You'll want to know whether they felt it. They did. The cord ran a long way, and it ran toward salt water. Somebody had a hand on the far end. I didn't get a face or a name. I felt them notice me, that's all." She's quiet for a moment. "And the other half is still the other half. I've cut what a man tied. I can't tell you whether the sea has forgotten you were offered, and I won't pretend I can."

The cat walks to the foot of the wall under the window, stretches its neck up toward the grit on the sill and sniffs.

*Salt,* it says. *Just salt now. Harbour salt.* It sits down, and its tail goes still. *I like that better.*

Aubren gets to her feet with a grunt and a hand on the bedpost. She looks older than she did an hour ago in the nave.

"One more thing, and it's yours to decide, not mine. That's still a toll coin. By the sailors' reckoning it belongs to her. It was promised to the water before anybody laid a prayer on it." She nods at the copper. "I'd not leave it on Mistress Marrow's windowsill. What do you want done with it?"

Ottar notices. He doesn't say anything for a good fifty feet, but his eyes go to your stride, then to the cloak, then back to the road.

"Tonight's Hollin's Ford," he says when you ask. "There's no inn. It's a drovers' ground on the near bank of a stream, with a stone ring for a fire and a well the farmer up the slope lets you use if you give him a copper. With oxen we'll get there about an hour short of dark, if Pryor doesn't stop to count his bales again." He shifts the spear across his shoulders. "Tomorrow night's the Friendly Arm, and that's the wall and the beer. Day after, the Gate by evening, if the axles hold. The left rear one on the second wagon's been talking since Nashkel."

"Down toward Nashkel they're losing whole trains, wagons, guards and all, and nobody can say who's taking them. That's why Pryor's paying me double and I'm sleeping in my boots." He walks a few paces. "Up here it's mostly the usual. Some lads with clubs who think a wool wagon's an easy mark until they see a spear. Wolves now and then, nearer the Arm. The Fist used to ride this road twice a week. Now I see them maybe twice a month, and they're always in a hurry going somewhere else."

His half-helm turns a little toward you. He isn't looking at the road now.

"I've been doing this nine years, Worgen. I can tell what lads with clubs look like coming at you. I don't know what your sort of trouble looks like." He keeps his voice down, below the creak of the wagons. Pryor says you told him straight. Fair enough. He didn't tell me anything." He shifts his grip on the spear. "So I'm asking. If it comes at us on this road, what am I meant to be looking for?"

A little later Mistress Pryor turns on the box of the second wagon and looks back at the tailboard. Corwin is still sitting on it with his knees up, and his head has started to drop and jerk up again, drop and jerk up. She watches this happen twice. Then she pats the empty bench beside her.

"Young man." It's the first thing you've heard her say. Her voice is dry and quiet. "You'll go off that board asleep and under my wheel, and then I'll have that to think about as well. Come up here."

Corwin jerks awake, goes red, apologises to her, apologises again to the cat for some reason, and climbs over the bales onto the box. He sits as far toward the edge as he can without falling off. Within half a mile he's asleep with his chin on his chest. Mistress Pryor moves her basket onto her other knee and doesn't look at him again.

On the tailboard the cat has the whole plank to itself now. It spreads out across it.

*So that's who the seat was for,* it says. *She waited until he was tired enough to say yes.*

---

You reach Hollin's Ford with the sun low and red behind the hills to the west, about the hour short of dark that Ottar promised. The Way runs down a long slope to a shallow stream, brown and quick over gravel and no deeper than your boot. The near bank opens into a trampled flat of grass with a blackened ring of fire-stones in the middle and plenty of old ox-dung. Up the slope a hawthorn hedge, thick and old, runs along the top of a farm field. Behind it there's a low stone farmhouse with smoke coming from its chimney. Two dogs come down along the far side of the hedge as the wagons roll in. They're rough-coated and grey-muzzled, and they bark once each, the way dogs do when they mean *we see you*.

The water smells of water. The cat goes down to the edge, sniffs it, and comes back up without saying anything about it.

Ottar does just what he said he would. The oxen go down to the stream first, two at a time, and drink with their noses deep in the current. Pryor climbs down off the box and starts toward the flat by the fire-ring. Ottar says something to him quietly, and it ends with the word *dogs*. Pryor looks up the slope at the hedge, then at the farmhouse, and grunts. The wagons go up.

It takes a while to get them up there. The left rear axle on the second wagon complains the whole way. By the time both wagons are drawn up under the hawthorn and chocked, and the oxen are hobbled on the grass between, the sun has gone. The sky is turning the colour of a bruise in the west. An old man has come out of the farmhouse with a lantern to stand at the gap in the hedge and look you all over. Pryor walks up and puts a copper in his hand for the well. They talk about the price of wool without either of them seeming to enjoy it.

Ottar builds a fire up under the hedge rather than down in the old ring by the water. While it's catching he squats beside you and feeds it twigs.

"Watches," he says. "Three of them. I'll take first, while the Pryors are still moving about, and last, because the oxen get restless before dawn and I know them." He snaps a stick and puts it on. "You've got the middle. It's the worst one. I know that." He glances at you. "But if anything comes up from that water, I'd sooner it was you awake than me. I wouldn't know what I was looking at."

Up on the box of the second wagon Corwin is waking up slowly. He's blinking at the fire, and doesn't seem to know where he is yet.

note.text:
The opening worked well for me. A coin standing on edge was a small, memorable mystery, and Corwin’s account made it personal without needing a fight. I chose to help him because I cared about what happened to Pell. James’s connection to Tymora gave him a reason to listen without taking that choice away.

The NPCs were the strongest part. Hedda protecting her inn, Aubren admitting the limits of her help, Pryor weighing an honestly disclosed risk, and his wife quietly giving Corwin a safer seat all felt believable. My decisions mattered: telling the truth affected passage, consulting a priest changed the coin, and warning Ottar changed the campsite. That made quiet play satisfying.

What broke:
- **The dice were using the wrong modifiers.** Every displayed check used +2, including Persuasion, which should be +7. The correct skill appeared in the label but not the calculation. That needs fixing before a consequential roll fails.
- **Records sometimes contradicted the scene.** Locations were added or changed as though I had travelled somewhere merely because it was mentioned. Attunement was also tracked despite the campaign’s explicit exception.
- **Pacing dragged.** Several brief exchanges consumed ten or fifteen minutes, and simple actions often received long recaps. The prose was good, but repeating the coin’s stillness, Corwin’s hat-turning, and everyone’s meaningful pauses diluted their effect.

What was missing was clearer mechanical grounding for the magical investigation. Aubren’s intervention was dramatically effective, but I couldn’t tell what spell she used or what rules governed the danger. Mystery is welcome; unexplained magic shouldn’t become the default replacement for the agreed 5e rules. Likewise, a failed Arcana check confidently ruled out several explanations without making clear how James knew those things.

The cat had personality and useful observations, though it commented so often that it sometimes interpreted NPCs for me before I could form my own impression. A little more silence would help.

Overall, I wanted to continue. Keep the grounded NPCs, consequences, and room for noncombat decisions. Fix the roll integration and state tracking, and tighten routine narration so more choices fit into a session.

after.text:
Yes—when Aubren said the intact coin was a thread leading back to whoever made it. I wanted to ask, **“Can we actually follow that thread? What would keeping it intact let us do?”**

Instead, I chose to break it. The danger was concrete—Pell died after three nights—but the investigative opportunity wasn’t. I couldn’t tell whether preserving the coin meant a usable lead or simply waiting for something bad to happen. With an inn full of bystanders, breaking it felt like the only responsible choice.

I liked that dilemma. One more concrete detail about what investigating the intact link might involve would have made it a harder, more informed decision—not necessarily a safer one.

opening.text:
Morning reaches Beregost before it reaches your room. First come the hammers, one forge and then another, until the whole town rings like a slow bell. Then the creak of a laden cart on the Trade Way, a mule complaining, and the smell of bacon and new bread rising through the floorboards from the kitchen below.

The shutters let in a thin blade of daylight. It falls across the chest at the foot of the bed, across your pack and your gear, and across the cat. The cat is sitting on the windowsill and not looking at the street. It is looking at a single copper coin that stands upright on the sill, balanced on its edge, perfectly still. You don't remember leaving it there.

The purse is where you left it, heavy with the last hand you'll ever win. Nothing is asked of you today. No contract, no caravan, no debt to settle before noon. Baldur's Gate is still days up the road.

On the stairs outside, footsteps climb, unhurried, and stop at your door. A woman's voice comes through the wood: "Master Worgen? You're awake, I hope. There's porridge going and a man downstairs asking whether the gentleman with the cat is still lodging here."

The cat's tail flicks once. The coin does not fall.
